common_name: Mulligan's Rambling Musk Rose (Giant Fragrant White Species Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring against a sturdy support, since this rambler eventually becomes enormous.

directions: This vigorous species rambler performs best in full sun but still flowers well in light to open shade, making it useful for softening a shaded wall or scrambling up a large tree. In a single flush each summer it produces broad clusters of small, fragrant, single white flowers followed by orange-red hips that persist into winter. Because mature plants can eventually reach 60 feet given a tall enough support, site it only where there is ample room to climb, and prune lightly after flowering just to remove dead or crowded wood.

common_name: Adelaide d'Orleans Rambling Rose (Blush-White Evergreen-Leaved Climber)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring in rich, well-drained soil against a fence, arbor, or small tree.

directions: A graceful once-blooming rambler descended from Rosa sempervirens, this rose produces abundant clusters of small, creamy blush-pink double flowers that fade to near white as they age, set against glossy, almost evergreen foliage. Give it full sun and rich, well-drained soil, with occasional watering once roots are established. It is most dramatic trained up a pergola or into an old tree, where the long flexible canes can drape and cascade for several weeks of late-spring bloom.

common_name: Autumn Sunset Shrub Rose (Golden Apricot Climbing-Sport Shrub)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring in rich, well-drained or sandy soil in full sun.

directions: Autumn Sunset arose as a golden-apricot sport of the popular shrub rose Westerland and shares its vigor and disease resistance while offering a warmer, sunset-toned flower color. Plant it in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water regularly through its first seasons to encourage repeated summer flushes. Left unpruned it builds into a large, arching shrub, but it also takes well to being tied to a support and grown as a short climber where more height is wanted.

common_name: Darlow's Enigma Rose (Continuous-Blooming Musk-Scented Found Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring in rich, well-drained or sandy soil; full sun gives the heaviest bloom.

directions: Of uncertain parentage and first noticed growing wild, Darlow's Enigma makes up for its mysterious origins with nearly nonstop clusters of small, single white flowers carrying a sweet musk fragrance that draws bees from spring through fall. It tolerates light to open shade, though flowering is heaviest in full sun, and rewards rich, well-drained soil and regular watering with strong, nearly thornless canes and excellent disease resistance. Allow it room to arch into a large, loose shrub, or train it as a modest climber against a fence or post.

common_name: Francis E. Lester Rambling Rose (Apple-Scented Single-Flowered Climber)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring in well-drained soil against a strong support with room to spread.

directions: This vigorous rambler flowers equally well in full sun or light, open shade, bearing huge trusses of single blush-pink flowers that fade to white and carry a distinct apple-like fragrance. The late-summer show continues into fall as the spent flowers give way to small orange-red hips that birds relish. Give it a fence, arbor, or small tree to climb into, since a well-grown plant can spread wider than it is tall, and prune only to remove old or damaged wood after the single big bloom flush.

common_name: Seagull Rambling Rose (Golden-Stamened White Climber)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring in rich, well-drained soil beside a tall support or mature tree.

directions: Seagull is an exceptionally vigorous rambler, equally happy in full sun or light, open shade, that smothers itself in early summer with large sprays of semi-double white flowers set off by bright golden stamens. Its long, pliable canes are easiest to manage when trained up into an old tree or over a substantial pergola, where it can climb 25 feet or more. Water occasionally once established in rich, well-drained soil, and expect only a single, spectacular flowering period each year rather than repeat bloom.

common_name: Beverly Shrub Rose (Fragrant Pink Kordes Repeat-Bloomer)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring in fertile, well-drained soil; it tolerates light to open shade but flowers best in full sun.

directions: Bred by the German house of Kordes, Beverly forms a tidy, upright shrub that repeats its show of large, fragrant pink flowers from spring through summer. It holds up well in smaller gardens thanks to its compact habit and good disease resistance, and tolerates a bit more shade than many modern shrub roses without losing much vigor. Keep the soil consistently moist through the growing season and deadhead spent blooms to encourage the next flush.

common_name: Day Breaker Shrub Rose (Fryer-Bred Repeat-Blooming Compact Shrub)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring in fertile, well-drained soil; tolerates light to open shade but flowers best in full sun.

directions: One of the newest Great Plant Picks rose selections, Day Breaker was bred by the English firm of Fryer's Roses and grows into a neat, upright shrub well suited to small borders and mixed plantings. It carries its flowers in repeated flushes from spring through summer and, like several newer Fryer introductions, tolerates a little shade without sulking. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil and water regularly during the growing season for the strongest repeat performance.

common_name: Easy Spirit Shrub Rose (Patented Repeat-Blooming Compact Shrub)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring in fertile, well-drained soil; tolerates full sun or light shade.

directions: Protected under U.S. Plant Patent 30120, Easy Spirit is a modern landscape shrub rose bred for an upright, well-branched habit and steady repeat bloom from spring into summer. It adapts to full sun or light shade, making it a flexible choice for mixed borders where light conditions shift through the day. Grow it in fertile, well-drained soil with regular watering, and expect minimal disease trouble typical of the newest generation of landscape rose breeding.

common_name: Cyaneum Stonecrop (Gray-Green Mat-Forming Sedum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in well-drained or sandy soil in full sun.

directions: This low, spreading stonecrop carries rounded, fleshy, gray-green leaves on trailing stems that knit together into a dense carpet within a couple of seasons. In late summer and into fall it is topped with flattened clusters of small purple-pink, star-shaped flowers that attract bees and butterflies. Plant it in full sun in lean, fast-draining soil, where it will shrug off summer drought once established and needs almost no supplemental feeding or care.

common_name: Kimnachii Stonecrop (Chartreuse-Leaved Spreading Sedum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in well-drained or sandy soil in full sun.

directions: Kimnachii stonecrop forms spreading mats of glossy, spoon-shaped, chartreuse leaves that hold their bright color best in sunny, lean conditions. Its flattened clusters of golden-yellow, star-shaped flowers appear earlier than most border sedums, opening in early summer rather than fall. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil, and allow it to weave between stepping stones or spill over a rock garden ledge where its unusual foliage color can be appreciated up close.

common_name: Primrose-Leaf Dwarf London Pride (Shade-Tolerant Saxifrage Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or fall in rich, well-drained soil in light to deep shade.

directions: A dwarf, more refined selection of London pride, this evergreen saxifrage forms neat rosettes of rounded leaves that slowly spread into a dense groundcover by way of short stolons. It tolerates even deep shade for foliage alone, though its airy, open sprays of small flowers are showiest when a bit more light reaches the plant. Grow it in rich, consistently moist but well-drained soil at the front of a shaded border or along a woodland path edge, where its compact scale fits spaces too small for the larger species.

common_name: Dentata Toothed-Leaf Saxifrage (Evergreen Shade Groundcover Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or fall in humus-rich soil in light, open, or dappled shade.

directions: This low hybrid saxifrage spreads into broad rosettes of evergreen, sharply toothed leaves that give it a crisper, more textured look than plain London pride. In spring it sends up delicate, airy sprays of small starry white flowers well above the foliage mat. Grow it in light, open, or dappled shade in humus-rich soil, watering only occasionally once it is established, and let it form a long-lived patch under shrubs or along a shaded path where its foliage texture can be a year-round asset.

common_name: Spring Beauty Dutch Crocus (Lavender with Violet Flame Petals)

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Spring Beauty is a large-flowered Dutch crocus hybrid whose soft pastel-lavender petals carry a bold violet flame down the outside, giving each goblet-shaped bloom extra presence in the early garden. Plant the corms in fall in well-drained soil in full sun, where they naturalize readily and return in increasing numbers over the years. Let the foliage die back naturally after bloom to recharge the corms for the following spring, and consider planting it through a lawn area that can go unmown until the leaves yellow.

common_name: Yellow Mammoth Dutch Crocus (Large Buttercup-Yellow Goblet Blooms)

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: True to its name, Yellow Mammoth produces unusually large, rich buttercup-yellow goblet flowers with matching anthers, making it one of the showiest of the large Dutch crocus hybrids for early spring color. Plant corms in fall in full sun and well-drained soil, where they multiply steadily and brighten lawns, borders, and rock gardens alike before most other bulbs have begun to bloom. Allow the grassy foliage to fade naturally after flowering so the corms can store energy for next year's display.

common_name: Blue Eddy Ornamental Onion (Swirling Blue-Green Foliage Allium)

planting.note: Plant bulbs or divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Blue Eddy is grown chiefly for its foliage: tidy, symmetrical rosettes of blue-green leaves that twist and swirl as they grow, giving the clump an almost sculptural quality even before it flowers. In summer, rounded heads of soft mauve blossoms rise just above the foliage and draw a steady stream of bees and other pollinators. Plant it in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, where its compact, clumping habit makes it well behaved at the front of a border or in a rock garden, unlike seedier ornamental onions.

common_name: Album Autumn Crocus (Pure White Single-Flowered Colchicum)

planting.note: Plant corms in late summer in well-drained soil in full sun, since they often bloom within weeks of planting.

directions: This snow-white form of the autumn crocus sends up large, vase-shaped flowers directly from bare ground in early autumn, well before its strappy foliage appears the following late winter. Plant the corms shallowly in well-drained soil in full sun during late summer dormancy, since they can begin flowering within days of being set in the ground. The leaves persist through spring to recharge the corm before going summer-dormant again, so site it where its gap in foliage will be masked by neighboring perennials, and note that all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Little Miss Maiden Grass (Compact Crimson-Tinted Ornamental Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil.

directions: Little Miss is a notably compact maiden grass, staying a tidy 2 to 3 feet tall and wide, which makes it one of the few Miscanthus selections well suited to small gardens and containers rather than large borders. Its narrow foliage picks up crimson and maroon tones through summer before the whole clump turns warm fall color, and unlike most of its relatives it tolerates light to open shade without becoming floppy or sparse. Plant in average, well-drained soil in spring, water regularly while establishing, and cut the clump back hard in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Angustissima Fountain Bamboo (Magenta-Green Waxy-Culm Clumping Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained soil; no root barrier is needed since this bamboo is a tight, non-running clumper.

directions: Angustissima stands out among clumping bamboos for its new culms, which emerge a striking magenta-green dusted with a white, waxy coating before maturing to green. The softly arching canes and fine-textured foliage build into a tall, non-invasive clump that works well as a privacy screen in part shade or dappled light. Grow it in well-drained soil in full sun to dappled shade, and keep it evenly watered through its first few summers while the clump establishes its mature height.

common_name: Scabrida Fountain Bamboo (Persimmon-Sheathed Smoky Blue-Culm Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained soil with full sun and afternoon shade, or light shade overall.

directions: This vase-shaped clumping bamboo offers some of the most colorful culms of any Fargesia, with young canes in a smoky lavender-blue emerging from vivid persimmon-orange sheaths that persist for striking contrast. It forms a well-behaved, non-running clump that makes an excellent accent or narrow screen without the maintenance worries of running bamboo species. Give it full sun with afternoon shade, or light shade overall, in well-drained soil, and water regularly during establishment to support its aboveground display.
